newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss parliament debates central bank law changes.
newsitem.headline: Swiss parliament debates central bank law changes.

text.p: Switzerland's parliament began deliberations this week on proposed changes to the Swiss National Bank's SNB) legal charter which would give the central bank greater freedom in managing its resereves.
The SNB hopes to generate 400 million Swiss francs in additional income from better managing its assets.
The revision is unrelated to a planned revaluation of the SNB's gold reserves, which would finance a humanitarian fund for victims of the Holocaust.

The proposals, based on a report compiled by SNB and finance ministry officials, includes proposals to allow the central bank to use derivatives and invest in longer-dated and higher yielding debt of foreign states, banks or international organisations.
One of the main attractions of the revision is that it would allow the central bank to invest currency reserves in instruments with maturities of more than one year.
The lower house of parliament begins its debate on the proposals today. Its ruling on the law changes will be followed by discussions in the upper house.
The measures proposed are not controversial and assuming there is no great opposition to the plan, the revised laws could be in force by the end of the year, an SNB spokesman said.

He also pointed out that these proposals are separate and not related to a central bank plan to use official gold reserves held by the SNB to create a humanitarian fund for victims of the Holocaust and other recipients would entail selling gold over a 10-year period.
The federal government and the Swiss cantons, the principal owners of the central bank, are entitled to the proceeds from SNB's currency investments.
But at least one parliamentarian has proposed using some these profits to stock the planned humanitarian fund, a finance ministry spokesman said. -- Zurich Editorial +41 1 631 7340
